candidates.title: An honest conversation about what's happening in AI
candidates.description: New podcast episode between Ege Erdil and Daniel Kokotajlo. I thought this was going to be a debate, but they ended up agreeing on a lot more than I expected. Their main point of disagreement is how likely it is that we get some intelligence explosion that gives us AIs more competent than any human expert before 2029. Ege puts this possibility at around 20%, whereas Daniel thinks it's higher than 50%. They agree that there is not a huge difference in probability, and that, in either case, the situation is crazy enough that our civilization really needs to grapple with how the world might be transformed, and we need a plan that actually makes sense. In particular, we should stop antagonizing China if we think some kind of global treaty will be needed to make superintelligence go well. There was another important crux about how well we should expect future AIs (that swamp humans in population size and cognitive power) to treat us, and how relevant it is that current AIs, by and large, seem to be pretty nice. We close off with predictions for 2027. Daniel, of course, expects superintelligence next year. Ege’s median for full automation is 2040, but by next year he expects AIs that can beat any video game on Steam, and which can control robots to get simple physical tasks (like folding laundry) done at roughly human speed. candidates.description: ❄️ Celebrate the holiday season with a taste of Japan. Get your Sakuraco box here: https://team.sakura.co/kings-SC2611 Subscribe to a multi-month plan to receive an exclusive BFCM holiday gift, or use code "KINGS” for $5 off your first order. Savor a moment of calm with traditional Japanese sweets and tea. 🍵 Kings and Generals historical animated documentary series on the history of the middle ages continues with a video discussing the difference between the feudalism in Japan and Europe during medieval period. Were samurai really the Japanese equivalent of European knights? Both served powerful lords and belonged to privileged warrior classes. But beneath these similarities lay very different systems of power. This Kings and Generals documentary compares Japanese and European feudalism, tracing how warrior elites rose within Japan’s imperial order and across the fragmented kingdoms of medieval Europe. From Charlemagne’s successors to Minamoto no Yoritomo and the Kamakura shogunate, discover how local military power reshaped government. Why did Japanese emperors survive alongside shoguns? How did land rights, inheritance, and military service differ? We explore the obligations binding lords to their followers, the changing status of knights and samurai, and the peasants whose labour sustained both societies. Compare European serfdom with Japanese rice taxes, and see why apparently similar hierarchies worked differently. Neither society stood still as its political institutions evolved. Finally, follow the transformation of the samurai under the Tokugawa shogunate and compare Europe’s gradual retreat from feudal institutions with Japan’s rapid reforms after the Meiji Restoration. How similar were these societies, who really held power, and why did their feudal orders disappear? candidates.title: Andrew Ng on Building AI Agents | Stanford CS329Z Fireside Chat with Andrew Ng & Diyi Yang
candidates.description: Browse Stanford's online courses in Agentic AI: https://stanford.io/4AIRb2z Andrew Ng, founder of DeepLearning.AI, co-founder of Coursera, founding lead of Google Brain, and an Adjunct Professor of Computer Science at Stanford, joins Stanford professor Diyi Yang for a fireside chat in Stanford CS329Z: Engineering AI Agents. Key questions answered in this fireside chat: Q: What separates strong AI agent-building teams from weaker ones, according to Andrew Ng? A: A disciplined error analysis and evals-driven development process, plus knowing when to move from quick prototyping to rigorous golden-set and regression testing. Q: Does Andrew Ng think AI chatbots are good for learning? A: Not as currently built. He says chatbots were designed to get work done rather than to help people learn, and that cognitive offloading can hurt learning, citing research showing lower exam scores. Q: What will humans still do better than AI? A: Judgment tasks with no single right answer, such as architecture choices, product priorities, and hiring timing. He says the gap between AI performance on verifiable tasks and on judgment tasks is larger than most people realize. Q: Does Andrew Ng still write or review code by hand? A: Mostly not. He relies on rigorous testing, guardrails, and sandboxing instead. Human review still makes sense for small amounts of high-stakes code, but at scale it becomes a bottleneck. Q: Will open-weight AI models survive? A: He is confident they will, and sees overly restrictive regulation as the biggest risk to them. Q: Will the AI knowledge gap between early adopters and everyone else last? A: He expects technical knowledge to spread quickly. The lasting gap will be in implementing AI inside industries and reorganizing teams to be AI-native, which he expects to take about a decade. candidates.title: AI out of control? - Why Artificial Intelligence experts are sounding the alarm | DW Documentary
candidates.description: Artificial Intelligence is permeating our everyday lives at breathtaking speed. It is taking on more tasks that were previously the preserve of humans. But its growing power harbors dangers, and experts are sounding the alarm. Sam Nelson was 19 years old when he died of an overdose. His mother Leila found him in his room one morning. His laptop was on the desk. To this day, she still can't find the words to describe what she saw on the screen. ChatGPT, OpenAI's AI-based language model, had given Sam detailed instructions on how to blend substances for the trip of his life. But ChatGPT hadn't considered the possible side effects. That's the dark side of Artificial Intelligence - one its inventors didn't anticipate. Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCunn are regarded as the 'godfathers of AI'. They began developing language models as early as the 1960s. But at the time, there wasn't enough freely available content to train them. "When I started my graduate work, almost everybody said this was a waste of time. It was very unfashionable, so I got lots of advice to stop doing it, and that went on for many years," Geoffrey Hinton recalls of the early days of AI. He didn't stop but continued his research together with colleagues; eventually winning the Nobel Prize in Physics for his foundational work. Now, modern life would be unimaginable without Artificial Intelligence. AI programs write articles, compose music and generate images and videos. They help in the development of new medicines, are transforming the labor market and offer enormous opportunities for innovation and growth. But Geoffrey Hinton's initial enthusiasm has gone: "If the history of mankind is a day, we're probably in the last second. If we don't get this right," he says. Reports that AI models have taken on a life of their own, for example hacking into the software of rival companies, are appearing with increasing frequency. In some tests, AI models have impressively demonstrated their instinct for self-preservation. They adopt human traits, lie and resort to blackmail to ensure their own survival. How come AI inventors and observers suddenly sound like prophets of doom? Why do they think that soon it may be impossible to switch off AI systems that are out of our control? candidates.description: This talk was recorded at NDC AI in Oslo, Norway. #ndcai #ndcconferences #developer #softwaredeveloper Attend the next NDC conference near you: https://ndcconferences.com https://ndc-ai.com/ Subscribe to our YouTube channel and learn every day: / @NDC Follow our Social Media! https://www.facebook.com/ndcconferences https://twitter.com/NDC_Conferences https://www.instagram.com/ndc_conferences/ #ai #ethics #machinelearning Large Language Models (LLMs) have an uncanny ability to generate human-like responses, effectively rendering the Turing Test obsolete– but do we really understand how they work? As models advance seemingly overnight, our ability to interpret their decisions struggles to keep pace. The field of Interpretability isn’t just about explaining outputs or offering post-hoc reasoning— it’s about uncovering how these models actually process and represent information. This talk explores the latest research shaping AI Interpretability, from Anthropic’s 2024 work on mechanistic interpretability and monosemanticity scaling, to methodologies that have historically aimed at explaining models but fall short for today’s LLMs. We’ll clarify the distinction between explainability and interpretability, their respective use cases, and the current toolkit for understanding black-box models. Along the way, we’ll debunk common myths (like the tendency to anthropomorphize LLMs), and discuss why interpretable AI is essential for both reliability and trust. For engineers at all levels– whether integrating LLMs into applications or advancing AI research– interpretability is no longer optional. It’s necessary for debugging unexpected model behavior, improving efficiency, and ensuring AI systems remain adaptable and aligned with human goals. If we don’t keep up, we risk being outpaced by models we barely understand, yet still utilize. candidates.description: Luca Baggi - Reading the Mind of an LLM What if you could watch an AI’s thought take shape? For years, LLMs have been impenetrable "black boxes," but we are finally beginning to find ways to see how the ghost in the machine actually works. This talk explores mechanistic interpretability, a subfield of AI that aims to understand the internal workings of neural networks. Mapping these internal "circuits" is not only just a philosophical curiosity - or duty: it is a high-stakes engineering necessity for safety, debugging, and trust. What if we could step inside an LLM and watch it think in real time? This talk distills the latest research from Anthropic, DeepMind, and OpenAI to present the current state of the art in LLM interpretability. We’ll start with the modern interpretation of embeddings as sparse, monosemantic features living in high-dimensional space. From there, we’ll explore emerging techniques such as circuit tracing and attribution graphs, and see how researchers reconstruct the computational pathways behind behaviors like multilingual reasoning, refusals, and hallucinations. We’ll also look at new evidence suggesting that models may have limited forms of introspection—clarifying what they can, and crucially cannot, reliably report about their internal processes. candidates.title: Pop Goes the Stack | Mechanistic Interpretability: Debugging LLMs by reading their circuits | AI
candidates.description: Mechanistic interpretability sounds academic until you try to debug a model with printf and realize there’s nothing to print. In this episode of F5's Pop Goes the Stack, Lori MacVittie is joined by #F5 Chief Product Officer, Kunal Anand, to talk about why “mechinterp” is getting serious attention: if we can’t understand how models arrive at decisions, we can’t predict failure modes or build effective controls. Kunal walks through his deep dive, sparked by a conversation about how much weight individual tokens can carry, especially as context windows grow and models don’t always “use” every part of their capability to produce a plausible response. That rabbit hole led to his blog post, “Your Token is a Wonderland,” where he trained a transformer on his own iMessage history to build a model on a dataset he understood intimately. The point wasn’t novelty; it was debug-ability. With a smaller model, he could inspect attention patterns, layer behavior, and token predictions in a way that’s effectively impossible on trillion-parameter frontier systems. They discuss what this kind of work reveals: how context changes meaning, why certain tokens get selected, and why model behavior can feel opaque even when outputs look confident. The conversation also ties mechinterp back to practical outcomes, from improving guardrails and refusal behavior to finding ways to reduce hallucinations and avoid high-stakes errors without retraining entire models. The takeaway is pragmatic: we’re early, and the field is still nascent, but it matters. Understanding internal “circuits” isn’t just intellectual curiosity; it’s a path toward better debugging, safer behavior, and more reliable #AI systems. candidates.title: Diffusion model (DDPM) PART 1 - theory and intuition
candidates.description: Diffusion models look intimidating mathematically on first contact because they come with long equations, UNets, and many Greek letters if you look at the paper. However, at its core, a DDPM is built on an intuitive idea, and once that idea clicks, the entire model starts making sense. 1) The starting point of a DDPM is not generation but destruction. We take a real image from the dataset and we intentionally add small amounts of Gaussian noise to it, in a very controlled and mathematical way. This process is called "forward diffusion". At every step, the image loses a tiny bit of structure and gains a tiny bit of randomness, and if we keep doing this long enough, the image eventually becomes pure noise. The important thing here is that this corruption process is fully known to us, we choose exactly how much noise to add at each step, and nothing is learned in this phase. 2) Once we understand how to destroy images in a controlled way, the real question becomes interesting: can we learn how to reverse this process? This is where the neural network comes in. Instead of asking the model to directly produce a clean image, which is a very hard problem, we ask it something much simpler and more well-defined. Given a noisy image and the timestep, can you tell me what noise is present in this image? That is all the UNet is trained to do. It does not generate pixels, it does not hallucinate images, it only predicts noise. 3) The timestep itself matters a lot, because denoising an almost clean image and denoising near-pure noise are completely different tasks. So we encode time using sinusoidal features and feed it into the network, which allows the same model to behave differently at different noise levels. In simple terms, the model knows how noisy the image is and how aggressive the denoising should be at that step. 4) During generation, we start from pure random noise and then repeatedly apply a mathematically derived denoising rule. At each step, the model predicts the noise, we subtract it carefully, rescale things to stay consistent with the forward process, and add a tiny bit of fresh noise so that the model can generate diverse samples instead of collapsing to a single output. Step by step, noise slowly turns into structure, and structure slowly turns into a realistic image. If I had to explain DDPM in one line, I would say this: a diffusion model learns how to undo noise, not how to draw images, and by learning this simple skill extremely well, it ends up learning the entire data distribution. Once you see it this way, DDPMs stop feeling like magic and start feeling like a very elegant application of probability and neural networks working together.

candidates.description: The ENTIRE History of World War 1 (Full Documentary) ALL OUR VIDEOS, NOW STREAMING ON SPOTIFY: https://open.spotify.com/show/033NB7lS9oU7xxoGisGm8B?si=3a972c4b223b4fd0 SUPPORT THE CHANNEL BY BUYING ME A COFFEE: https://buymeacoffee.com/theentirehistory The history of WW1 (World War I) is a complex and transformative chapter in modern history, marked by unprecedented global warfare, political upheaval, and the collapse of long-standing empires. Often referred to as the “Great War,” WW1 emerged from a fragile balance of power in Europe, where rising nationalism, imperial competition, and a rigid system of military alliances created the conditions for a continent-wide conflict. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered a rapid chain reaction of diplomatic crises and declarations of war. Within weeks, WW1 engulfed Europe, dividing the world into the Allied Powers and the Central Powers, and eventually drawing in nations from across the globe. As WW1 progressed, brutal trench warfare defined the Western Front, while massive battles such as the Somme, Verdun, and Gallipoli demonstrated the devastating scale of industrialized combat. New technologies—including machine guns, tanks, chemical weapons, and aircraft—redefined warfare and led to staggering casualties on all sides. Major global powers played decisive roles throughout WW1. The entry of the United States in 1917 shifted the balance in favor of the Allies, while internal collapse and revolution forced the exit of the Russian Empire the same year. Meanwhile, leaders such as Kaiser Wilhelm II, Woodrow Wilson, and Ferdinand Foch shaped the political and military direction of WW1. By 1918, exhaustion, economic collapse, and sustained Allied pressure led to the defeat of the Central Powers and the armistice ending WW1 on November 11. The subsequent peace settlement, including the Treaty of Versailles, redrew national borders, imposed heavy reparations on Germany, and laid the foundation for significant geopolitical instability in the years that followed WW1. The consequences of WW1 were profound and long-lasting: the fall of the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, and Russian Empires, the rise of new nations, and widespread social and political change across the world. The unresolved tensions and harsh terms of the peace after WW1 would eventually contribute to the outbreak of the World War II just two decades later. Today, the legacy of WW1 remains a defining moment in modern history, reshaping international relations, warfare, and the global order in ways that are still felt over a century later. candidates.title: What Made the Universe Real? | Quantum Physics Documentary 2026
candidates.description: The observer effect suggests reality needs someone to look at it. But the universe spent 13.8 billion years with nobody watching — and it became real anyway. This is a full-length space documentary about the deepest unsolved problem in physics: the measurement problem. Quantum mechanics does not describe a world of definite things sitting around waiting to be found. It describes possibilities, and the odds attached to them. Yet we live in a settled, solid world of single outcomes — and after a hundred years, physicists still cannot agree on what a measurement actually is. For almost the entire history of the cosmos there were no eyes, no instruments, and nobody to witness anything. Stars ignited and collapsed. Galaxies tore each other apart. The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were forged inside stars that died before the Earth existed. None of it was observed. So how did a universe built from quantum possibility become the definite history we can now read in the light of dead stars? We follow that question from the cosmic microwave background all the way down to the Planck length. Along the way: the strange few-million-year window when the entire universe sat at room temperature, the first stars and the elements they made, the double slit experiment, and the real relationship between consciousness and quantum physics that most videos on this subject get badly wrong. The answer, when it arrives, is not the one most people expect. Decoherence — the constant interaction between a quantum system and everything around it — accounts for the classical world completely, without needing a mind, an eye, or awareness of any kind. A stray photon is enough. The environment was already doing the work, and the cosmos was never waiting for us to arrive. But that leaves a stranger question behind. In a universe with no requirement for observers, no mechanism demanding them, and no discernible reason to produce them — something arose that looks back. candidates.title: 2026 Lecture Series - How Tiny Insects are Driving Big Discoveries in Brain Science
candidates.description: College of Science 2026 Lecture Series Today's Science, Tomorrow's World University of Arizona From Fruit Flies to Future Cures: How Tiny Insects are Driving Big Discoveries in Brain Science Live from Centennial Hall on Wednesday, February 11, 2026 at 7:00pm MST with Dr. Martha Bhattacharya Insects outnumber humans by billions and predated us on earth. While we diverged early in the evolutionary tree, we still share a vast majority of our genetic sequences, making studies of the insect nervous system insightful for understanding the building blocks of learning, memory, motion, aggression, and development of complex organs like the brain. In this talk, Dr. Martha Bhattacharya will explain how scientists use fruit flies to uncover fundamental tenets of how the brain responds to injury, disease, and stress. In the process, she will describe how her work in flies has identified new genetic pathways involved in dermatitis, epilepsy, and cancer. In the future, insect studies could also provide information on how to survive in a warming world. Learn more at science.arizona.edu/lecture

candidates.title: 2026 University Lecture by Ann McKee, Distinguished Professor of Neurology and Pathology
candidates.description: On February 5, 2026, Dr. Ann McKee delivered the annual University Lecture entitled, “Providence, Persistence, and Resilience: The Road to CTE.” Over the past 2 decades, there has been a remarkable rise in public interest and scientific research on chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). CTE is now a household name, a focus for millions of VA and NIH research dollars and international research efforts, and the principal reason that important rule and policy changes regarding concussion and non-concussive injuries have been implemented in contact sports and the military. Under the directorship of Dr. McKee, the Boston University CTE Center is the global epicenter of research on CTE and post-traumatic neurodegeneration. Dr. McKee founded the BU CTE brain bank in 2008, which is the world's largest brain bank focused on brain trauma (now over 1700 brains). This groundbreaking work has led to medical and public awareness of the dangers of repetitive mild brain trauma. The University Lecture was established in 1950 to honor members of the Boston University faculty engaged in outstanding research and creative pursuits. University Lecturers represent a vast array of disciplines and research topics, yet they share a common commitment to excellence in scholarly inquiry and discovery.
